receipts.how: The sole NT occurrence, where the word is absorbed into the wider phrase 'walking worthy of the Lord unto all pleasing,' confirms the positive-to-neutral sense the definition describes.

The word's integration into Pauline paraenesis rather than standing alone confirms it names an aim or effort to please, consistent with the definition's framing of intentional conduct toward another's satisfaction.
Abbott-Smith and Moulton-Milligan both cite this verse as Paul's positive use, parallel to the A.D. 137 papyrus, validating the definition's claim that NT usage diverges from the classical bad sense.

why: ἀρέσκω occurs 17 times in the Byzantine (Majority) New Testament, across 8 books.

The Majority Standard Bible — translated from this same Greek text — renders it “please” in 9 of those places (53%), e.g. Matthew 14:6; Mark 6:22. This is observed translation data, not an editorial opinion.
The Berean Standard Bible, an independent translation, agrees with that rendering in 100% of the same verses.
The sense “please” is independently listed by Dodson, the KJV glosses, corroborating the corpus evidence.
In the Septuagint it appears 39 times, most often translating the Hebrew יָטַב (H3190) (14×).
Moulton–Milligan documents this word in everyday papyri and inscriptions, anchoring the meaning in ordinary Koine usage outside the New Testament.
Good confidence: solid sample with corroborated or dominant primary sense.

prose.def: To please someone, or to act so as to win their favor — often by rendering willing service for their benefit.
senseLabels: to please or seek to please
prose.article: At its core ἀρέσκω means to please someone, and that single sense covers all 17 New Testament occurrences, rendered "please" in 9 of them. But there's a richer shade behind the word: in everyday Koine it often carries the idea of actively serving others' interests rather than just pleasing oneself. Moulton-Milligan points to monumental inscriptions where ἀρέσκω describes citizens who "proved themselves of use to the commonwealth," which lines up with passages like Romans 15:1-3 and 1 Corinthians 10:33 where the focus is on benefiting others. In the Septuagint it appears 39 times, most often translating the Hebrew יָטַב ("to be good, go well").

issues: The single sense label '1. to please or seek to please' collapses what Abbott-Smith and Moulton-Milligan distinguish as two distinct uses: (1) to please a person and (2) to render service in another's interest; these are treated as separate senses in the classical lexicons and map to distinct NT passages

The rare renderings (e.g., 'man please', 'man concerned affairs', 'approval striving please') and the Galatians 2× occurrences strongly suggest a 'people-pleasing' nuance (seeking human approval) that the current definition softens with 'often' and does not flag as a distinct shade

The syntactic role data reports 'vocative (17×)' which is almost certainly a data artifact for a verb lemma, but the definition does not account for any syntactic variability; more importantly, the definition makes no distinction between the reflexive 'please oneself' versus 'please another' polarity that Paul explicitly exploits (ROM 15:1-3)

The supporting article's LXX claim that ἀρέσκω 'most often' translates יָטַב is undermined by the supplied data: יָטַב appears 14× but that is the most frequent single Hebrew equivalent — the definition should not be built on this LXX grounding without noting the spread across multiple Hebrew roots

receipts.how: Paul's rhetorical question 'Am I now seeking the approval of men or of God?' shows the 'people-pleasing' nuance the current single-label definition does not adequately capture.

Paul writes that 'we who are strong ought not to please ourselves' — illustrating the service-to-others sense that Abbott-Smith and Moulton-Milligan mark as a distinct second use, absent from the current sense label.

Paul contrasts pleasing God versus pleasing men in a context of ministerial integrity, confirming that the word carries an active 'rendering service / seeking approval' dimension beyond simple pleasing.

audit.author_note: Paul (Romans, 1 Corinthians, Galatians, 1 Thessalonians) consistently uses ἀρέσκω in theologically charged antitheses — pleasing God versus pleasing humans — while Matthew and Mark use it in purely narrative contexts of a performance that delighted a ruler, making the theological 'service' nuance a distinctly Pauline deployment.
